title: Triads
goal: Know what a triad is, play major and minor triads in three places on the top strings and on the middle strings, and move between the chords of a song with the nearest shapes.
assumes: You can fret and pick single notes and play eighth notes with a click at 60 BPM, and you can find C on the B string or will learn it in the first Exercise. No theory is assumed: this Path starts from counting the notes of one scale. If you have done Know the Neck and Scales and Modes you already know the note names and the major scale, and the two Steps that count scales will go quickly. The minutes listed are one pass through the material; these shapes are worth months.

skills: Eighth notes with a click at 60 BPM

orderRationale: The major scale counted as numbers comes first, because a triad is defined by them: notes one, three and five. Then the three shapes one triad has on the top three strings, one at a time, since the top strings are the easiest to hear and to hold. The count is done again in F and in G before those two chords get their shapes, so their letters are worked out and not handed over, and the Beginner Level ends on whole tunes of eight and twelve bars. Moving one shape to make three chords comes before the nearest-shape idea: it is easier, and it shows that a shape is a chord type and a fret is a chord name. Minor arrives as one changed note, never as a new set of shapes to memorise. The four chords most songs use come next, in two parts of the neck and then in other keys, before a second set of strings: a second set before the first is secure doubles the load and teaches nothing new. Seeing the open and barre chords as these same three notes comes near the end, when the three notes are familiar enough to recognise. A whole song form is last, and then a longer one in a new key that uses two sets of strings as two colours. The middle strings close the Intermediate Level, with F, G and the minor chords drilled there as they were on the top strings, because Chords in a Key leans on them; the A, D and G strings wait for the Advanced Level, after the first two sets have been joined.
gradingLimits: Every graded Exercise is played one note at a time: after the take, the app checks that you played the written notes, counts them and times them. It cannot tell which string a pitch came from, so a right note in the wrong place passes, and it cannot hear whether you held the shape down like a chord or lifted each finger. Strummed chords are not graded anywhere in this Path. The band Exercises have only been tried on computer-made guitar sound, so direct input or headphones are the honest way to play them. Choosing your own shapes is 'your turn', self-checked and labelled 'not checked yet'.

steps.title: One, three, five
steps.goal: Count the C major scale along one string, pick out its first, third and fifth notes, and play those three under one hand.
steps.why: A chord is not a shape someone invented. Take a major scale, count its notes from one to seven, and play numbers one, three and five together: that is a major chord, and the three notes are called a triad. Every major chord you already play is three notes like these, some of them played more than once. Once you can count to five on one string, you can build a chord anywhere.
howTo: The words this Path uses. The strings, from thickest to thinnest: low E, A, D, G, B and the top string. Fret 1 is the first space next to the nut, at the head end of the neck. Fingers are numbered from the index finger: first, second, third, and the little finger is the fourth.

A click is the tick of the metronome. Each tick is a beat, four beats make a bar, and BPM is how many beats go by in a minute. A whole note lasts a whole bar, a half note two beats, a quarter note one beat. The pass tempo is the speed at which an Exercise counts as done.
The C major scale is C, D, E, F, G, A, B, and then C again. Count them: C is one, E is three, G is five.
On one string, a scale is a row of frets. On the B string, C major is frets 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 13.
One is called the root, and it gives the chord its name. Three is the third and five is the fifth. The C at fret 13 is one again, an octave up: the same note, higher.
steps.payoff: You can say what a C chord is made of, and play its three notes without looking them up.

exercises.title: Count the scale on the B string
exercises.purpose: The C major scale along one string, up and back, so each note has a number. One finger does all of it, which leaves your attention for counting.
howTo: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
B string, first finger only: frets 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 13, then back down to fret 1. Say the numbers as you go up: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and one again at fret 13.
Most notes are two frets apart, which is called a whole step. Two pairs are only one fret apart, a half step: three and four (frets 5 and 6), and seven and the top (frets 12 and 13).
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and steady quarter notes after the take. The app can't hear you count, so that part is yours.

cues.say: Say each note's number as you play it.
Move one fret only from three to four.
Press right behind the fret, then pick.
Pick each note once, on its click.
Move to the next fret before the click.
Wait for the click before each new note.
Look at the next fret before you move.
Come down to fret one and hold it two beats.

exercises.title: One, three and five on one string
exercises.purpose: Only the first, third and fifth notes of the scale: C, E and G. Played alone they already sound like a chord, and the C at fret 13 is one again, higher.
howTo: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90. B string, first finger only.
Bars 1 and 2: frets 1, 5, 8, 5, then 1, 5, and 8 held. That is C, E, G. Bars 3 and 4 start from the high C at fret 13: 13, 8, 5, 8, then 13, 8, and 5 held.
Say each note's number as you play it: bars 1 and 2 go one, three, five, three, and bars 3 and 4 go one, five, three, five.
exercises.coachLine: Three notes, a long way apart on one string. Right notes after the take.

cues.say: Say each note's number: one, three or five.
Play the high C at fret thirteen.
Press right behind the fret, then pick.
Pick each note once, on its click.
Move to the next fret before the click.
Wait for the click before each new note.
Count fret eight's two beats, then jump up.
Look at the next fret before you move.
End on fret five and hold it two beats.

exercises.title: The same three notes under one hand
exercises.purpose: C, E and G again, on three strings this time, so the hand does not have to travel: C on the G string, E on the B string, G on the top string. This is a triad shape.
howTo: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
G string fret 5 with the third finger, B string fret 5 with the fourth, top string fret 3 with the first. Put all three down and leave them down.
Play low, middle, high, middle, and in bar 2 stop on the high note. Say 'one, three, five, three'.
exercises.coachLine: The first triad shape. Right notes and steady quarters after the take.

cues.say: Put all three fingers down and leave them down.
Fourth finger on the B string, fret five.
Press the whole shape down before you pick.
Pick each note once, on its click.
Pick each note right on its click.
Wait for the click before each note.
Count the high note's two beats, then go on.
Keep the pick close as it crosses strings.
Hold the top note for beats three and four.

steps.title: Three shapes for one chord
steps.goal: Play the C triad in its three shapes on the top three strings and know which of its notes is on top in each.
steps.why: C, E and G can be stacked three ways on three strings: with C lowest, with E lowest, or with G lowest. Each way makes a different small shape, and the three shapes sit one after another up the neck, so between them the chord is never more than a few frets from your hand. They are the same chord: the letters do not change, only the order. Musicians call them inversions.
howTo: Shape one, around fret 5: C, E, G from low to high. Shape two, around fret 8: E, G, C. Shape three, around fret 12: G, C, E. Shape one has the root as its lowest note, shape two the third, shape three the fifth, and that holds for every chord.
The lowest note of one shape moves to the top of the next. Watch the C: it is on the G string, then on the top string, then on the B string.
Hold each shape down like a small chord and pick the strings one at a time.
steps.payoff: C major in three places, and you can say which note is on top of each.

exercises.title: Shape one and shape two
exercises.purpose: The shape you know at fret 5, and the next one up: G string fret 9, B and top strings at fret 8. Two bars each, so the hand has time to settle.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bars 1 and 2: G string 5 (third finger), B string 5 (fourth finger), top string 3 (first finger), rolled low, middle, high, middle. Bars 3 and 4: G string 9 with the second finger, B string 8 and top string 8 under the first finger laid flat.
In shape one the top note is G, the fifth. In shape two the top note is C, the root.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

cues.say: Look at fret eight before you leave shape one.
Lay finger one flat across fret eight.
Press the whole shape down before you pick.
Pick one string on each eighth, no more.
Have the next shape ready before '1'.
Wait for '1' before the new chord's first note.
Start each change on the last eighth.
Keep the pick close as it crosses strings.
Keep shape two down to the last note.

exercises.title: Shape two and shape three
exercises.purpose: From the shape at fret 8 to the one at fret 12: G string 12, B string 13, top string 12. In shape three the top note is E, the third.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bars 1 and 2: G string 9, B string 8, top string 8. Bars 3 and 4: the first finger lies across fret 12 on the G and top strings, and the second finger takes fret 13 on the B string.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take.

cues.say: Look at fret twelve before you leave shape two.
Finger one on fret twelve, G and top strings.
Press the whole shape down before you pick.
Pick one string on each eighth, no more.
Have the next shape ready before '1'.
Wait for '1' before the new chord's first note.
Start each change on the last eighth.
Keep the pick close as it crosses strings.
Keep shape three down to the last note.

exercises.title: All three, up and back
exercises.purpose: One bar on each shape: fret 5, fret 8, fret 12, and back to fret 8. The chord stays C the whole way while the sound climbs.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bar 1: frets 5, 5, 3. Bar 2: 9, 8, 8. Bar 3: 12, 13, 12. Bar 4: 9, 8, 8 again. The G string's fret is given first each time.
Move the whole hand at the bar line, and look at the fret you are going to before you leave.
exercises.coachLine: Three shapes and a shift at every bar line. Right notes and even eighths after the take.

cues.say: Lead with the G string: five, nine, twelve.
Say C, E, G as you fret each shape.
Press the whole shape down before you pick.
Pick one string on each eighth, no more.
Have the next shape ready before '1'.
Wait for '1' before the new chord's first note.
Look at the next fret before you move.
Keep the pick close as it crosses strings.
Come back to shape two right on '1'.

steps.title: One, three, five in F and in G
steps.goal: Count the F major scale and the G major scale along the top string, pick out the first, third and fifth notes of each, and play each three under one hand.
steps.why: You counted one scale, C, and its first, third and fifth notes made a C chord. F and G are the next two chords you need, and they are made the same way, each from its own scale. Count the F major scale and its one, three and five are F, A and C. Count the G major scale and they are G, B and D. Doing the count again turns those letters into something you worked out, before the next Step gives the two chords their shapes.
howTo: In the first Step, C major on the B string was frets 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 13: two frets between most notes, and one fret between three and four and between seven and the top. Every major scale has those same gaps, whatever note it starts on.

F is fret 1 of the top string, so F major on the top string is the same row of frets: 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 13. G is fret 3, so G major is that row two frets higher: 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 15.

Keeping the gaps changes one letter in each scale. In F the fourth note is one fret above A, and that note is B flat, the note one fret below B. In G the seventh note is one fret below the top G, and that note is F sharp, the note one fret above F.
The fourth note of F is called B flat and not A sharp because a scale uses each letter once and A is already taken. For the same reason the seventh note of G is F sharp and not G flat.
One, three and five are not the fourth note or the seventh, so neither chord has the changed note in it: F is F, A, C and G is G, B, D.
As with C, one is the root and names the chord, three is the third and five is the fifth.
steps.payoff: You can say why an F chord is F, A and C and a G chord is G, B and D, and you can find each under one hand.

exercises.title: Count the F major scale on the top string
exercises.purpose: The F major scale along the top string, up and back, with a number for each note. The frets are the ones C major had on the B string, because F is at fret 1 here as C was there.
howTo: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Top string, first finger only: frets 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 13, then back down to fret 1. Say the numbers as you go up: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and one again at fret 13.
The letters are F, G, A, B flat, C, D, E and F. Three and four are one fret apart, so four is at fret 6, and that note is B flat. B itself is at fret 7.
One is F at fret 1, three is A at fret 5 and five is C at fret 8.
exercises.coachLine: The count of the first Step, from a new note. The counting aloud is still yours. Right notes and steady quarter notes after the take.

cues.say: Say each note's number as you play it.
Play four at fret six: B flat.
Press right behind the fret, then pick.
Pick each note once, on its click.
Move to the next fret before the click.
Wait for the click before each new note.
Look at the next fret before you move.
Come down to fret one and hold it two beats.

exercises.title: One, three and five of F: one string, then one hand
exercises.purpose: F, A and C picked out of the scale on the top string, then the same three notes on three strings, where one hand holds them. The shape is shape one, the fingering C has at fret 5, five frets higher: G and B strings at fret 10, top note at fret 8.
howTo: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bars 1 and 2, top string, first finger only: frets 1, 5, 8, 5, then 1, 5, and 8 held. That is F, A, C: one, three, five.

Leave the first finger on fret 8. Bars 3 and 4: put the third finger on the G string at fret 10 and the fourth finger on the B string at fret 10. From low to high that is F, A and C, with the C you were already holding on top.
Bars 3 and 4 go low, middle, high, middle, then low, middle, and the high note held. Say 'one, three, five, three'.
exercises.coachLine: One string, then one hand. The app hears the same three notes in all four bars, so the move to three strings is yours to check. Right notes and steady quarters after the take.

cues.say: Keep finger one on fret eight into the shape.
Third finger on the G string, fret ten.
Press the whole shape down before you pick.
Pick each note once, on its click.
Pick each note right on its click.
Wait for the click before each note.
Count fret eight's two beats, then the G string.
Look at the next fret before you move.
Keep the pick close as it crosses strings.
Hold the top note for beats three and four.

exercises.title: Count the G major scale on the top string
exercises.purpose: The G major scale along the top string from fret 3, up and back. It is the row of frets you played for F, two frets higher.
howTo: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Top string, first finger only: frets 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, then back down to fret 3. Say the numbers as you go up: one to seven, and one again at fret 15.
The letters are G, A, B, C, D, E, F sharp and G. Seven and the top are one fret apart, so seven is at fret 14, and that note is F sharp. F itself is at fret 13.
One is G at fret 3, three is B at fret 7 and five is D at fret 10.
exercises.coachLine: The same count once more, from G. The counting aloud is still yours. Right notes and steady quarter notes after the take.

cues.say: Say each note's number as you play it.
Play seven at fret fourteen: F sharp.
Press right behind the fret, then pick.
Pick each note once, on its click.
Move to the next fret before the click.
Wait for the click before each new note.
Look at the next fret before you move.
Come down to fret three and hold it two beats.

exercises.title: One, three and five of G: one string, then one hand
exercises.purpose: G, B and D picked out of the scale on the top string, then on three strings under one hand. It is shape one again: G and B strings at fret 12, top note at fret 10.
howTo: Quarter notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bars 1 and 2, top string, first finger only: frets 3, 7, 10, 7, then 3, 7, and 10 held. That is G, B, D: one, three, five.
Leave the first finger on fret 10. Bars 3 and 4: put the third finger on the G string at fret 12 and the fourth finger on the B string at fret 12. From low to high that is G, B and D.
Bars 3 and 4 go low, middle, high, middle, then low, middle, and the high note held.
The F sharp of the G scale is not in the chord, and the B flat of the F scale was not in F: a chord takes only one, three and five.
exercises.coachLine: One string, then one hand. The app hears the same three notes in all four bars, so the move to three strings is yours to check. Right notes and steady quarters after the take.

cues.say: Keep finger one on fret ten into the shape.
Third finger on the G string, fret twelve.
Press the whole shape down before you pick.
Pick each note once, on its click.
Pick each note right on its click.
Wait for the click before each note.
Count fret ten's two beats, then the G string.
Look at the next fret before you move.
Keep the pick close as it crosses strings.
Hold the top note for beats three and four.

steps.title: F and G in three places
steps.goal: Play the three shapes of F major and of G major on the top strings, and play C, F and G by moving shape three.
steps.why: You learned the three shapes on one chord. They are not C shapes: they are major shapes, and every major chord has the same three, in the same repeating order up the neck. Each chord comes into that order at a different shape and fret. Doing it again for F and for G is what turns three fingerings into something you know. These are also the two chords you will need next.
howTo: F is F, A, C. Start on shape three at frets 5, 6, 5, then shape one at 10, 10, 8, then shape two at 14, 13, 13. Shape two also fits near the nut, at 2, 1, 1: the small F chord you may already know.
G is G, B, D. Shape two comes first: 4, 3, 3. Then shape three at 7, 8, 7, then shape one at 12, 12, 10.
Shape one always has the root lowest, shape two the third, shape three the fifth. Which shape comes first on the neck depends on the chord.
steps.payoff: Three major chords, each in three places: nine shapes from three fingerings.

The letters are F, A and C every time.

Have the next shape ready before '1'.
Wait for '1' before the new chord's first note.
Start each change on the last eighth.
Keep the pick close as it crosses strings.
Come back to the middle shape right on '1'.

exercises.title: G major in three places
exercises.purpose: The three shapes of G up the neck and back: around fret 3, around fret 7, around fret 11.
howTo: Straight eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. One bar on each shape.
Bar 1: G string 4, B string 3, top string 3. Bar 2: 7, 8, 7. Bar 3: 12, 12, 10. Bar 4: 7, 8, 7 again.
The letters are G, B and D every time.

Keep the pick close as it crosses strings.

exercises.title: C, F and G with shape three
exercises.purpose: One fingering, shape three, on three chords: C at fret 12, F at fret 5, G at fret 7, and back to C. The first finger holds the G string and the top string at the same fret, and the second finger holds the B string one fret higher.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90. One bar on each chord: C, F, G, C.
C: G string 12, B string 13, top string 12. F: 5, 6, 5. G: 7, 8, 7. Keep the fingers in their shape as the hand slides.
The band is a drummer and a bassist in place of the click.
If you get lost, stop, find beat 1 of the next bar and come back in there.
One fingering can be three chords because the shape makes a major chord wherever you put it, and the fret decides which one. The next Step works on that.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. Right notes and time after the take.

cues.say: Keep finger one across the G and top strings.
Finger two on the B string, fret six, for F.
Press the whole shape down before you pick.
Pick one string on each eighth, no more.
Have the next shape ready before '1'.
Wait for '1' before the new chord's first note.
Keep the fingers in shape as the hand slides.
Keep the pick close as it crosses strings.
Hold the C shape down to the last note.

steps.title: One shape, three chords
steps.goal: Play C, F and G by moving one shape, then by staying in one place and changing shape, over a band.
steps.why: A shape is a kind of chord, and the fret you put it on is the chord's name. Move the C shape up five frets and it is F; two more and it is G. That is the easy way to change chord. The better way is the opposite: stay where you are and change to the shape of the next chord that is already under your hand. Both are worth having, and the second is what makes a rhythm part sound smooth.
howTo: A key is the seven notes of one major scale, with the note you count from as home. The key of C is the C major scale.

Build a chord on notes one, four and five of the C scale and you get C, F and G: the first, fourth and fifth chords of the key of C, and the three chords of a great many songs. F is F, A, C and G is G, B, D.
Moving one shape: C at fret 5, F at fret 10, G at fret 12, counted on the G string.
Staying put around fret 8: C is 9, 8, 8. F is 10, 10, 8. G is 7, 8, 7. The top string hardly moves.
When a Take passes, play the same four bars once more with the three strings of each shape strummed together, two strums a bar. The app does not grade strums, so that part is yours to judge.
steps.payoff: Three chords over a band, played two ways, and the same three in three more keys.

Keep the top string's fret for one and four.

steps.title: One note makes it minor
steps.goal: Turn a major triad into a minor one by lowering its third, and play A minor in three shapes.
steps.why: The difference between a major chord and a minor chord is one note moved one fret. Lower the third and C major becomes C minor: the root and the fifth stay exactly where they were. So there are no new shapes to memorise. Find the third in a major shape you know, pull it back a fret, and you have the minor shape.
howTo: In shape one of C (frets 5, 5, 3), the third is E on the B string. Move it from fret 5 to fret 4 and the chord is C minor: E has become E flat, the note one fret lower.
A major is A, C sharp and E. Lower the C sharp one fret to C and you have A minor: A, C and E. A minor shares two of its three notes with C major: only the G has become an A.
Listen for the change of mood when the third moves. That one fret is the whole difference.
steps.payoff: You can hear and play the one fret that separates major from minor.

steps.title: The top note is a melody

steps.why: When you change chord, a listener follows the highest note. If it jumps about, the part sounds like separate chords; if it steps or stays, the part sounds like music. Because every triad has three shapes, you can nearly always pick one whose top note is next door to the last one. Musicians call this voice leading, and it is most of what makes a small chord part sound finished.

Low version: the top line is G, G, A, A, all at frets 3 and 5.

The idea has not changed: three notes, three orders, three shapes. The shapes themselves are a little different, because the B string is tuned differently from the others.
howTo: C on the middle strings: all three at fret 5 (G, C, E), which is shape three. Then D string 10, G string 9, B string 8 (C, E, G), shape one. Then 14, 12, 13 (E, G, C), shape two.
A minor: D string 7, G and B strings 5 (A, C, E). Then 10, 9, 10 (C, E, A). Then 14, 14, 13 (E, A, C).
Let the underside of the finger on the B string lean lightly on the top string so it stays quiet.
steps.payoff: Every triad you know, in a second, warmer part of the guitar's range.

steps.title: F and G on the middle strings
steps.goal: Play the three shapes of F major and of G major on the D, G and B strings, and play C, F and G there without leaving one part of the neck, in C and in other keys.
steps.why: On the top strings you learned the shapes on C and then gave them to F and G. The middle strings get the same treatment, for the same reason: a shape you have played on one chord is a fingering, and a shape you have played on three is something you know. These three shapes are the major shapes of this set of strings, and they come in the same repeating order up the neck as before: root lowest, third lowest, fifth lowest, and round again, with each chord coming into that order at a different shape.
howTo: F is F, A, C. On the D, G and B strings, D string first: 3, 2, 1 is shape one. 7, 5, 6 is shape two. The first finger across fret 10 is shape three.
G is G, B, D: the same three shapes two frets higher. 5, 4, 3, then 9, 7, 8, then the first finger across fret 12.
Shape three is one finger laid flat, which makes it the easiest to move and the easiest to let buzz. Press with the bony edge of the finger, close to the fret.
steps.payoff: C, F and G in three places each on a second set of strings, and one, four and five there in four keys.

steps.title: Two sets of strings, one chord
steps.goal: Join the middle-string shape and the top-string shape of a chord into one four-string shape, and move one C triad all the way up the neck and back.
steps.why: The shape on the middle strings and the shape on the top strings in the same place share two strings. Put them together and you have four strings of the chord under one hand, which is most of the way to the full chord shapes you may already know. And because every shape leads to the next, one chord can be walked from the bottom of the neck to the top.
howTo: Around fret 5, C on the middle strings is 5, 5, 5 and C on the top strings is 5, 5, 3: together, D string 5, G string 5, B string 5, top string 3.
The four-string shape has one note twice: here G is on the D string and on the top string.
Roll up through four strings, back down, and play one more note on the G string to finish the bar.
steps.payoff: Four strings of any chord under one hand, and C major from fret 3 to fret 14.

steps.title: The A, D and G strings
steps.goal: Play C major and A minor in three shapes on the A, D and G strings, and the four chords there.
steps.why: One more set of strings, one lower again. Down here a triad is thick and dark: it is the sound of a rhythm guitar under a singer, and of the low end of every barre chord. These three strings are tuned the same distance apart, with no B string to bend the pattern, so the shapes are new once more. They are also the last new shapes: the low E, A and D strings are tuned the same distance apart and take the same fingerings, so after this set there is no triad shape on the guitar you have not played.

A minor: 3, 2, 2 is C, E, A. 7, 7, 5 is E, A, C. 12, 10, 9 is A, C, E, with the root lowest.
Rest the side of the picking hand on the low E string so it stays quiet under these shapes.

steps.title: Three chords down low, and three sets in one place
steps.goal: Play C, F and G on the A, D and G strings, move the four chords there to other keys, and play one C chord on all three sets of strings without moving the hand.
steps.why: A new set of strings is only yours once it has carried more than one chord and more than one key. And there is something to see now that you have all three sets: in any one part of the neck, the same chord sits on each of them, one above the other. Lay the three over one another and you have five strings of a barre chord; add the low E string and it is the whole chord. You have been playing pieces of it all along.

Around fret 8, C is 10, 10, 9 on the A, D and G strings, 10, 9, 8 on the D, G and B strings, and 9, 8, 8 on the top three.
Lay those three over one another, sharing strings, and you have the C barre chord at fret 8 with only the low E string still to add: 8, 10, 10, 9, 8, 8.
steps.payoff: One chord on three sets of strings under one hand, and the low set in any key.

steps.title: The third kind: diminished

It sounds tense and unfinished on its own, and that is its use: it leans hard toward the chord a fret above its root. In the key of C the only one is B diminished, and it leads to C. In Chords in a Key it is the chord on the seventh note of the scale.

steps.title: The chords you know are triads
steps.goal: Find the triad inside an open C chord and a barre chord, and hear what one more note, the seventh, does to a chord.
steps.why: An open C chord has five strings and only three different notes: C, E, G, C, E. A six-string barre chord has only three as well. Every big major or minor chord shape is a triad with some notes played twice, which is why the small shapes you have learned sound like the same chord. Going the other way, add the seventh note of the scale to a triad and you have a seventh chord: the next family of chords, built the same way.
howTo: Open C, low to high: C (A string, fret 3), E (D string, fret 2), G (open G string), C (B string, fret 1), E (open top string).

The open chords of First Chords and Strumming hold shapes you have played. The top three strings of open D, 2, 3, 2, are shape three of D. The D, G and B strings of open A minor, 2, 2, 1, are the A minor shape from 14, 14, 13, twelve frets lower. The top three strings of open C, 0, 1, 0, are shape three of C from fret 12, twelve frets lower. The small F is shape two of F.
If you play barre chords: a G barre chord at fret 3 is, low to high, G, D, G, B, D, G. Its top three strings are the G triad you know: 4, 3, 3.

B is the seventh note of the C scale: add it to C, E and G and you have C major seven. Lower it one fret to B flat and you have C seven. On three strings you leave out G, the fifth, which the ear does not miss, and keep C and E with the new note on top.
steps.payoff: You can look at a chord shape and name the three notes it is made of, and you have heard what a seventh adds. Chords in a Key and Arpeggios over Changes take the sevenths further.

levels.title: Intermediate: minor, the nearest shape, and the middle strings
levels.summary: Minor as one lowered note, A minor, D minor and E minor in three places each, the four chords most songs use in two parts of the neck and in other keys, choosing shapes so the top note makes a line, and then all six chords of the key again on the D, G and B strings. After this Level you have everything Chords in a Key assumes.

startHereIf: You can play a C major triad in 3 places on the top strings at 80 BPM.
You can play C, F and G with triads over a band.
You change chord by moving the whole hand, and your parts sound jumpy.

warmups.title: One major shape, three chords
warmups.purpose: One of the three major shapes on the top strings, rolled on the first, fourth and fifth chords of a key and home. A different shape and key each time.
howTo: Straight eighths, well under your clean tempo. Keep the fingers in their shape and move the whole hand at the bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

cues.say: Start well under your clean tempo.
Sound all three notes of every chord.
Have the new chord ready before '1'.
Wait for '1' before the new chord's first note.
Start each change on the last eighth.
Keep the pick close to the strings.
Keep the eighths even right to the last note.

levels.title: Advanced: every set of strings, and whole chords
levels.summary: Two sets of strings joined into four-string shapes, the same triads on the A, D and G strings, one chord on all three sets, the diminished triad, the triads inside open and barre chords, seventh chords, and two songs: eight bars, then sixteen. After it, Arpeggios over Changes plays these same chords as lines.

startHereIf: You can play C, A minor, F and G with the nearest shapes on the top strings at 90 BPM.
You can say the top note of each of the 3 shapes of a triad.
You know triads on the top strings and on the D, G and B strings, and can't yet see them inside the chords you strum.

warmups.title: One minor shape, three chords
warmups.purpose: One of the three minor shapes on the top strings, rolled on three minor chords, the first, fourth and fifth, and home. A different shape and key each time.
howTo: Straight eighths, well under your clean tempo. Keep the fingers in their shape and move the whole hand at the bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

Keep the eighths even right to the last note.

warmups.title: One middle-string shape, three chords
warmups.purpose: One of the three major shapes on the D, G and B strings, rolled on the first, fourth and fifth chords of a key and home. A different shape and key each time.
howTo: Straight eighths, well under your clean tempo. Keep the fingers in their shape and move the whole hand at the bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.
